title: Reviewing someone else's change
objective: By the end of this lesson you can review a change usefully — reading it in the right order, knowing what to look for, and writing comments that improve the work instead of defending your taste.

blocks.text: Reviewing is a skill separate from writing code, and it is the one most people are never taught. A good review catches the defect that tests missed and leaves the author better informed. A bad review either waves the change through or turns into an argument about brace placement.

items: The description: what is this change for? If you cannot tell, that is your first comment
The tests: what does the author believe this does, and which cases did they consider?
The main change: does it actually do that, in a way that will still make sense in a year?
The edges: empty input, failure of the thing it calls, two users doing it at once
Then, last and least, style — most of which a formatter should be handling anyway

blocks.title: Start from the tests, not the diff
blocks.text: Tests state intent. Reading them first tells you what the author was trying to do, so you can review the implementation against that rather than against your own guess. It also makes missing cases obvious — the ones nobody wrote a test for are usually the ones that break.

rows: What happens when this list is empty?
If that call times out, what does the user see?
Where does this value come from, and is it trusted?
Is this delete reversible? Is it scoped to one account?
Two requests arrive together — does this still hold?
Will the next person understand why, or only what?
This also renames something unrelated — separate change?

blocks.text: Say which kind of comment it is

blocks.caption: A convention worth adopting
lines: blocking: this deletes rows for every account, not just the current one
question: is the retry safe if the first attempt partially succeeded?
suggestion: this reads more clearly as a guard clause — your call
nit: spelling in the log message
praise: the fallback path here is genuinely well handled

blocks.text: Prefixes remove the biggest friction in review: the author cannot tell what must change from what you merely prefer. Without them, every comment reads as a demand, and authors either argue or comply with all of it resentfully.

blocks.title: Review the change, not the person
blocks.text: 'This function is confusing' invites defence. 'I could not work out when the second branch runs — can you add a comment or split it?' invites a fix. Same observation; one is about the code and offers a way forward. Write the second one, especially when you are tired.

items: Approve when you understand the change and believe it is safe to ship
Say what you did not review — 'I read the API layer; I did not check the migration' is useful and honest
Do not approve a change you did not understand; ask instead. An approval you did not mean is worse than a delay
Request changes for anything blocking, and be specific about what would unblock it

blocks.title: Reviewing is how you learn a codebase
blocks.text: Reading other people's changes teaches you a system faster than reading it cold, because every change comes with an explanation of why it exists. New team members who review early become useful sooner — which makes it worth including them before they feel ready.
Reviewing locally when the diff is not enough

blocks.caption: Some changes have to be run
lines: git switch --detach origin/fix/upload-limit    # look without creating a branch
# run it, run the tests, try the failure cases yourself
git switch -                                   # return to your own work
git diff main...origin/fix/upload-limit        # the change as a whole
git log --oneline main..origin/fix/upload-limit # the commits, in order

blocks.title: Review a change as if you did not write it
steps: Make a small change with a deliberate gap — for example, handle only the success case
Run: git add . && git commit -m "Add the lookup helper" && git push -u origin feature/review-me
Run: git diff main...feature/review-me     (read it as a reviewer, top to bottom)
Write down three comments using the prefixes: one blocking, one question, one nit
Run: git switch feature/review-me and address your own blocking comment with a new commit
blocks.expected: Your own change read as an outsider, three comments in the prefixed style, and a follow-up commit fixing the blocking one. Reviewing your own work at a distance is the cheapest way to practise the habit.

cheatsheet: Read in order: description → tests → main change → edge cases → style last
Tests state intent; reading them first shows what the author meant to do
Look for correctness, failure handling, security, data safety, concurrency, readability, scope
Prefix comments: blocking / question / suggestion / nit / praise
Comment on the change, not the person, and offer a way forward
Say what you did not review — partial review honestly stated is useful
Never approve what you did not understand; ask instead
git switch --detach origin/<branch> to run a change locally before approving

checkpoint.prompt: What should you read first when reviewing a change?

choices.A: The largest file in the diff
choices.B: The description and the tests, because together they state what the change is meant to do
choices.C: The style issues, to get them out of the way

checkpoint.explanation: Reviewing an implementation without knowing its intent means reviewing it against your own assumption. Intent comes from the description and the tests.

checkpoint.prompt: Why prefix review comments with blocking / question / suggestion / nit?

choices.B: So the author can tell what must change from what you merely prefer, instead of reading every comment as a demand

checkpoint.explanation: Unlabelled comments force the author to guess your severity. That guessing is where most review friction comes from.

checkpoint.prompt: You do not understand part of a change well enough to judge it. What is the right action?

choices.A: Approve it and trust the author
choices.B: Ask a question, and state which parts you did review

checkpoint.explanation: An approval means 'I understand this and believe it is safe'. Asking, plus being honest about your coverage, is more useful than a signature you did not mean.

checkpoint.prompt: Which comment is more likely to improve the code?

choices.B: I could not work out when the second branch runs — could you add a comment or split it?
choices.D: I would have done this differently

checkpoint.explanation: It names the specific difficulty and offers two concrete ways forward. The others describe a feeling and leave the author guessing at what to do.
